conceptTag: Why adding people can slow a team
readerTitle: Why two more cooks made Saturday slower
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당 주방, 소프트웨어 팀) + 실제 저작 (Brooks, 1975 『The Mythical Man-Month』). 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 사람을 더하면 일손은 나중에 늘고, 가르치고 맞추는 비용은 지금 바로 늘어난다. 그래서 늦어진 팀에 사람을 붓는 것은 늦어짐을 키우는 고리가 될 수 있다.
misconception: 일이 밀리면 사람을 더 넣으면 된다. 사람이 두 배면 속도도 두 배다.

sources.text: Brooks, F. P. (1975). The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering. Addison-Wesley. (Brooks's law)
식당과 소프트웨어 팀 사례, 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Brooks's law 문장("Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later")과 출간 연도 1975년을 원서로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 뜻을 풀어 썼습니다.
주방과 소프트웨어 팀의 적응 기간(수 주)은 설명용 가정이며 업계 통계가 아닙니다.

cards.title: Why two more cooks made Saturday slower
body: A busy bistro was running 25 minutes from order to plate on Saturday nights. The owner hired two new line cooks to fix it.
The next Saturday, tickets took 32 minutes. Same kitchen, same menu, more people. Nobody was lazy. The system just did what systems do.

image.label: A crowded restaurant kitchen with cooks bumping into each other
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 좁은 식당 주방에 요리사 다섯 명이 서로 부딪히고, 베테랑 요리사가 신입에게 설명하느라 팬에서 연기가 난다. 벽에 주문표가 길게 밀려 있음. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Saturday tickets are running late.
body: You own the bistro. Three experienced cooks handle the line. Saturday orders take 25 minutes and reviews mention the wait. Your next big Saturday is in five days.

options.text: Hire two new cooks and put them on the line this Saturday
options.feedback: You gain hands on paper but lose your best cooks' attention to training, right at the rush. That is a **delay**: the cost arrives now, the help arrives weeks later.

options.text: Trim the Saturday menu and prep more ahead; hire one cook and train them on quiet weekdays
options.feedback: You speed up this Saturday without new coordination costs, and you pay the training cost when the kitchen can absorb it. You've planned around the **delay** instead of being hit by it.

options.text: Bring in one experienced temp cook just for Saturday
options.feedback: A skilled cook needs less teaching, so the dip is smaller. But they still don't know your stations or plates, so expect some friction on the night.

cards.title: The help comes later. The cost comes now.
body: New cooks don't know where the shallots are, how the chef plates the duck, or when to call "behind". For weeks they need guidance.
That guidance comes from the three people who were already the fastest. So output dips before it rises. This is a **delay in the system**: the gap between an action and its full effect.
If you judge the decision by next Saturday, adding people looks like a mistake. If you judge it in two months, it may look fine.

image.label: Line chart: team output dips after new hires, then rises
image.brief: 단순한 선 그래프. 가로축 "Weeks after hiring", 세로축 "Plates per hour". 채용 직후 선이 아래로 꺼졌다가 몇 주 뒤 원래 수준을 넘어 올라감. 꺼진 구간에 "Training cost" 라벨.

cards.title: Every new person adds more than one connection.
body: Each pair of people who must coordinate is a line of communication. With **n** people there are n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 pairs. Headcount grows in a line. Coordination grows much faster.

cards.title: Late, so add people. Slower, so add more.
body: Put the delay and the coordination cost together and a **reinforcing feedback loop** can form. The team is late. Managers add people. Training and coordination slow everyone down. The team gets later. Managers add more.
Fred Brooks saw this on large software projects and wrote about it in *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975). His rule, now called Brooks's law: adding people to a late software project makes it later.

image.label: Loop diagram: late, add people, more coordination, later
image.brief: 원형 화살표 다이어그램. "Behind schedule" → "Add people" → "More training and coordination" → "Less real work done" → 다시 "Behind schedule". 고리 가운데 "+" 표시로 강화 고리임을 나타냄.

cards.title: Now it's a software team.
body: Your five engineers are three weeks behind on a release a big client is waiting for. Your VP offers four engineers from another team, starting Monday.

options.text: Take all four and split the remaining work nine ways
options.feedback: Nine people means 36 pairs to coordinate, and the newcomers need your senior engineers to learn the codebase. This is the **reinforcing loop** Brooks described.

options.text: Cut scope with the client to ship the core on time; take one engineer for a separate, well-defined piece
options.feedback: Cutting scope removes work instead of adding coordination. One person on a cleanly separate task needs little hand-holding, so the **delay** is short.

options.text: Decline all help and ask the team to work weekends
options.feedback: You avoid onboarding costs, but tired people make more mistakes and bugs feed back as rework. It can start a different loop.

cards.title: Adding people often works. Timing is the trick.
body: Brooks's law is a rule of thumb, not a ban on hiring. More people help when the work splits cleanly, like a second dishwasher or a separate feature, and when newcomers already know the tools.
They also help when you add them early, so the training dip ends before the crunch. The mistake is not hiring. It's hiring late and expecting the payoff right away.

cards.title: People add capacity later and coordination now.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Delays in systems**: the help from new people arrives weeks after the cost. **Feedback loops**: late teams that add people can get later, which tempts them to add more.
**Try it today:** think of the last person who joined your team. How many weeks until they made the team faster, and who paid for those weeks?
